entries.content: The library currently exposes 39 types (the feature text itself doesn’t name them). I’m grouping them by whether they model software structure/behavior directly, support engineering planning/operations, or are mainly presentation/strategy visuals.

The library currently supports 39 diagram types. Most can relate to software work, but only a subset directly describes software systems.

One important clarification: this is not a conventional rendering library with a structured diagram DSL. It is an agent skill and template system that produces self-contained HTML containing inline SVG and CSS. Static output is the default. [Repository and diagram catalog](https://github.com/cathrynlavery/diagram-design)

### Recommended core types

These provide the most value in software design documentation:

| Type | Software-development use |
|---|---|
| Architecture | Components, services, stores, external systems, and connections |
| Flowchart | Algorithms, validation, branching business logic |
| Sequence | API calls, events, authentication, asynchronous interactions |
| State machine | UI, workflow, job, connection, or domain-state lifecycles |
| ER / data model | Conceptual entities, fields, and relationships |
| Database schema | Physical tables, types, constraints, indexes, and foreign keys |
| Deployment | Runtime zones, hosts, containers, artifacts, ports, and replicas |
| Dependency graph | Module, package, service, or build dependencies; cycles and fan-in |
| Data flow | How information moves and transforms through the system |
| Swimlane | Processes involving several services, users, or teams |
| Process | Ordered multi-actor workflows and handoffs |
| Layer stack | Application layers, abstractions, or security controls |
| Nested | System boundaries, ownership, scopes, and containment |
| Tree | File structures, syntax trees, configuration, or hierarchical data |
| High-Level | Simplified end-to-end system or data-platform overview |

I would make these the primary supported set for F_228.

### Useful in particular domains

These are valuable, but their applicability depends on the project:

| Type | Best use |
|---|---|
| UML class | Object-oriented domain and class design |
| IT current-state | Legacy-system inventories and modernization |
| Medallion | Bronze/silver/gold analytical data architecture |
| DP integration | Data-platform sources, core services, and consumers |
| DP security matrix | Role/component permissions and access reviews |
| Sankey | Quantified traffic, cost, event, or data-volume movement |
| Fishbone | Incident and defect root-cause analysis |
| User journey | Product discovery and UX design |
| Story map | Features organized into user activities and release slices |
| Wardley map | Build-versus-buy and technology strategy |
| Timeline | Incident reconstruction, migrations, and release history |
| Gantt | Release, migration, or infrastructure project planning |
| Kanban | Work tracking and bottleneck visualization |
| Quadrant | Risk/impact/effort prioritization |
| Org chart | Code ownership, escalation, and team responsibility |

### Mainly metrics or presentation

These can visualize engineering data, but they are charts rather than software diagrams:

- Bar chart: test failures, latency comparisons, defect counts.
- Line chart: performance, adoption, incidents, build duration over time.
- Scatter plot: performance correlations and benchmark distributions.
- Treemap: repository size, bundle composition, or cost allocation.
- Radar/spider and polar charts: maturity or capability comparisons.
- Pyramid/funnel: conversion pipelines or issue triage drop-off.
- Venn: overlapping responsibilities or capabilities.
- Loop/flywheel: feedback cycles such as develop → deploy → observe → improve.

These should probably be delegated to a general charting capability unless F_228 explicitly intends to cover quantitative visualization.

### Suggested scope

For an initial implementation, I recommend these 12:

1. Architecture
2. Flowchart
3. Sequence
4. State machine
5. ER/data model
6. Database schema
7. Deployment
8. Dependency graph
9. Data flow
10. Swimlane
11. Layer stack
12. Nested

They cover structure, behavior, data, runtime topology, dependencies, ownership boundaries, and workflows without turning the feature into a general-purpose charting system. The library itself also advises selecting diagrams only when they communicate more effectively than prose or a table. [Selection guide](https://github.com/cathrynlavery/diagram-design/blob/main/skills/diagram-design/SKILL.md)
